entries.meaning: Standing alone, hardly rejects a claim as far off the mark — it means "not remotely," not "barely." It is a dry, slightly bookish way to disagree, and it usually answers something the speaker considers an overstatement.
examples: "Was the movie scary?" "Hardly. I fell asleep."
"You must have been furious." "Hardly. I thought it was funny."
"So he's an expert?" "Hardly. He read one article on a plane."
"That's got to be the hardest class in the department." "Hardly — the final is open-book."
"That must have cost a fortune." "Hardly — forty bucks at an estate sale."

entries.meaning: Two different jobs depending on delivery. Said lightly it is a hedged no — polite, provisional, easy to argue with. Said flat and slow with the weight dropped on think, it is a hard refusal with a warning inside it: the speaker has caught you trying something. I think not is the stiff, jokey-formal cousin.
examples: "Is he coming with us?" "I don't think so, he's got class."
"Do we need to bring anything?" "I don't think so."
He reached for the last of the fries. "I don't think so."
"I'll just add the charge to your account." "I don't think so. We agreed on a flat rate."
"You'll let this one slide, right?" "I don't think so."

entries.meaning: A soft, friendly refusal of something offered — food, a drink, a ride, help with the boxes. It declines without ever using the word no, and it implies that the speaker already has what they need, so it lands as easygoing rather than blunt.
examples: "Want another slice?" "I'm good, thanks."
"I can drive you to the airport." "I'm good — I already booked a car."
"You need a hand with those boxes?" "Nah, I'm good."
"Should I order you a coffee?" "I'm good. I've had three already."
"Can I get you anything else?" "I'm all set, thank you."

entries.ipa: no settled IPA — a two-beat hum with the lips closed and a glottal catch between the beats, roughly /ˈm̩ʔm̩/, pitch falling from high to low
entries.meaning: The closed-mouth version of uh-uh: a nasal grunt that means no. The pitch pattern is what carries the meaning — high-then-low is no, while the low-then-high mm-hmm is yes, so the two are opposites that differ only in melody.
examples: "Did you touch the thermostat?" "Mm-mm."
She shook her head. "Mm-mm, that's not what he said."
"Anybody want the last one?" "Mm-mm." "Mm-mm."
"Mm-mm," he managed, mouth full of sandwich, waving the check away.
"Is this the right building?" "Mm-mm — it's the one across the street."

entries.respell: NA (rhyming with cat) or NAH; naw is NAW
entries.meaning: A relaxed, casual no — the everyday spoken negative among friends. It is softer and less final than no, and it usually trails a clause behind it that explains or cushions the refusal.
examples: "You coming out tonight?" "Nah, I'm beat."
"Naw, man, I already ate."
"Do you want me to wait for you?" "Nah, go ahead."
"Is it a big deal?" "Nah, it happens all the time."
"Nah, I don't think that's how the billing works."

entries.meaning: The Old English no, alive today in exactly two places: the recorded vote (the nays have it) and deliberately archaic joking. As an everyday refusal it dropped out of American speech centuries ago, so anyone who says it straight is either presiding over a meeting or doing a bit.
examples: "All those opposed?" "Nay."
The motion failed, nineteen nays to twelve ayes.
"Nay, good sir, I shall not be moved from this couch."
"Does the senator yield?" "Nay, Mr. Chairman."
"One more round?" "Nay — I'm driving."

entries.register: neutral (radio, aviation, military, and dispatch procedure); informal and jocular everywhere else
entries.meaning: The radio-procedure word for no, used where clarity matters more than tone: aviation, the military, police work, dispatch. Outside those settings Americans use it as a deadpan joke, and the hammed-up negatory is always a joke.
examples: "Do you have visual on the vehicle?" "Negative."
"Are you carrying any hazardous materials?" "Negative, tower."
"Negative — the shipment never left the warehouse."
"Did you remember the tickets?" "Negative." "You're kidding."
"You want anchovies on that?" "Negatory."

entries.meaning: As a one-word answer, never refuses for all time rather than just for now. It is emphatic by nature, so it tends to answer a question about the future or a proposal the speaker finds permanently unacceptable.
examples: "Would you ever move back?" "Never."
"Never. I'm not signing that."
"You'll thank me for this one day." "Never."
"Have you tried durian?" "No — and never."
"Come on, just one more game." "Never again. Last time took four hours."

entries.meaning: The base negative of English and the plainest refusal available in any register. Doubled or tripled (no no no) it turns urgent rather than merely negative; stretched out (nooo) it expresses dismay at something already happening rather than refusal of something proposed.
examples: "Is this seat taken?" "No, go ahead."
"No. I am not lending him the car again."
"No, no, no — you have to click Save first."
"Did anyone call while I was out?" "No, it's been quiet all morning."
"So you're fine with the change?" "No, and I said so in the meeting."

entries.meaning: The standard polite refusal of an offer. No thank you is the fuller and more formal version, no thanks is what most Americans actually say, and either one is a complete answer on its own.
examples: "More wine?" "No thanks."
"Would you like a bag?" "No thank you, I brought one."
"Can I interest you in the extended warranty?" "No thanks."
"We could split an appetizer." "No thanks — I want to save room."
"No thanks," she said, handing the flyer back.

entries.meaning: A crisp, casual no, closed off with a /p/ that makes it sound final and a little breezy. It suits flat factual answers and cheerful refusals to engage; tripled in a text (nope nope nope) it means "absolutely not, and I am backing away slowly."
examples: "Did the package come?" "Nope."
"Are you going to tell me what she said?" "Nope."
"Nope, that's not my department."
"Any chance they'll reschedule?" "Nope, the deadline's fixed."
She looked at the spider in the sink and typed nope nope nope into the group chat.

entries.meaning: The softest disagreement in ordinary American use. It answers in the negative while pulling most of the force out first, so it can decline, doubt, or contradict without closing anything off. It is also the standard polite way to say a thing was not good without ever saying it was bad.
examples: "Did you like the movie?" "Not really."
"Are you busy?" "Not really — what's up?"
"So that's how the tax works?" "Not really. It's messier than that."
"You must be thrilled." "Not really, to be honest."
"Have you two met?" "Not really — we've been on the same call a few times."

entries.respell: NUH-uh (first syllable stressed, pitch falling; the catch in the middle is the glottal stop of uh-oh)
entries.meaning: The playground contradiction: "that is not true." Where uh-uh simply answers no, nuh-uh denies a statement somebody has just made, and its natural sparring partner is uh-huh meaning "it is too." Adults use it jokingly, or when they are arguing like children on purpose.
examples: "You started it." "Nuh-uh, you did."
"Nuh-uh! I saw you take the last cookie."
"Dad said we could." "Nuh-uh, he said maybe."
"You've never even been to Texas." "Nuh-uh — I lived in Austin for a year."
"Nuh-uh," he said, grinning. "That is not what the rules say."

entries.meaning: Borrowed from card games and quiz shows, pass declines a turn, an invitation, or an offer. Hard pass is the emphatic version and carries a note of distaste — you are not merely declining, you want it on the record that you would never.
examples: "There's a karaoke thing after work." "Pass."
"Want to try the pickle soda?" "Hard pass."
"I'll pass on the Monday meeting — just send me the notes."
"Anyone want to present first?" "Pass."
"They want us in the office five days a week." "Yeah, that's a hard pass for me."

entries.meaning: The grunted no: two vowels with a catch in the throat between them, said high-then-low. It is the exact mirror of uh-huh ("yes"), which runs low-then-high, and melody is the only thing separating them — which is why learners get misheard on this one more than on almost any other word.
examples: "Did you finish the dishes?" "Uh-uh."
"Uh-uh, don't even think about it."
"Is that your car getting towed?" "Uh-uh, mine's the blue one."
"You want me to keep going?" "Uh-uh, that's plenty."
He held out the plate and the toddler clamped her mouth shut. "Uh-uh."

entries.meaning: The strongest refusal that is still safe in a meeting or an email. It closes the door completely without slang or profanity, which makes it the default emphatic no in professional settings.
examples: "Should I cc the whole team?" "Absolutely not."
"Are you suggesting we falsified the numbers?" "Absolutely not."
"Certainly not at that price."
"Can I put you down as a maybe?" "Absolutely not — I'll be out of the country."
"Definitely not," the doctor said. "Not while you're on this medication."

entries.meaning: A sardonic warning that the thing being hoped for is not going to happen, or at least not soon. It is skepticism aimed at somebody else's optimism rather than a refusal of a request.
examples: "They said they'd have it fixed by Friday." "Don't hold your breath."
"Maybe he'll finally apologize." "Don't hold your breath."
"The refund should post in three to five days." "Don't hold your breath — mine took a month."
"I'm sure somebody will call back." "I wouldn't hold my breath, honestly."
"Do you think the city will actually fix the potholes?" "Don't hold your breath."

entries.meaning: Said to somebody whose expectation you consider pure fantasy. Between friends it is teasing rather than cruel, and it can either refuse a request outright or mock a hope the other person has just voiced.
examples: "You're going to let me drive it, right?" "Dream on."
"I figure I'll be a manager by thirty." "Dream on."
"Keep dreaming — those tickets sold out in four minutes."
"Think they'll give us Friday off too?" "Dream on."
"So you'll cover my shift?" "Dream on, buddy."

entries.meaning: Means the opposite of what it looks like: a fat chance is no chance at all. The sarcasm is baked into the phrase itself, so it does not need any special tone of voice to be understood.
examples: "Maybe they'll upgrade us." "Fat chance."
"Fat chance of getting a table on a Saturday without a reservation."
"He said he'd pay you back this week." "Fat chance."
"Think the boss will even notice?" "Fat chance — he hasn't read an email in years."
"You could always ask for a raise." "Fat chance in this economy."

entries.meaning: Two jobs, both dismissive: it refuses a proposal flatly ("that is never happening"), and it waves away something that no longer matters ("never mind, drop it"). The eye-dialect spelling fuhgeddaboudit /fəˌɡɛdəˈbaʊdɪt/ covers both senses plus a third — "obviously, no question about it" — but be aware of what you are doing with it: it is an imitation of a working-class Italian-American New York accent, and outside New York it reads as a mob-movie impression.
examples: "Can I borrow the truck for the move?" "Forget it."
"What were you going to say?" "Forget it, it wasn't important."
"Forget about it — I'm not driving into the city on a holiday weekend."
"How much do I owe you?" "Forget it, it's on me."
"Is the pizza there any good?" "Fuhgeddaboudit. Best in Brooklyn."

entries.meaning: Sarcastic well-wishing. The speaker expects the plan to fail and is announcing, politely, that they will not be helping. The sincere version and this one are the same four words; what marks the sarcastic one is the flat delivery and the conspicuous absence of any offer to pitch in.
examples: "I'm going to ask him to reimburse me for the flight." "Good luck with that."
"We're driving to Boston the Wednesday before Thanksgiving." "Good luck with that."
"Good luck with that," she said, and went back to her own screen.
"I told them I need an answer by Monday." "Good luck."
"Apparently all four systems are supposed to talk to each other by the demo." "Ha. Good luck with that."

entries.meaning: A blunt, emphatic refusal carrying mild profanity. It is completely normal among friends and completely out of place in a client meeting; heck no is the safe substitute that keeps the shape and drops the edge.
examples: "Are you going to tell her yourself?" "Hell no."
"Hell no, I'm not paying eighteen dollars for parking."
"Would you do it again?" "Heck no."
"They want us to work Saturday." "Aw hell no."
"Did you sign anything?" "Hell no — I called a lawyer first."

entries.meaning: Refuses a request while mocking the asker for having hoped at all. It is a taunt as much as a refusal, so it presumes enough closeness to tease.
examples: "So you'll do my laundry too?" "In your dreams."
"I'm getting the corner office." "In your dreams."
"Give me a five-minute head start." "In your dreams — go."
"You'd let me win, right?" "In your dreams."
"In your dreams, pal. That seat's taken."

entries.meaning: A breezy "I can't do that," refusing on grounds of ability or rules rather than willingness. The clipped grammar is deliberate and frozen — it is never no can does and never takes a subject.
examples: "Any chance you can squeeze me in today?" "No can do — I'm booked solid."
"No can do, boss. The system locks after midnight."
"Can you hold the elevator?" "No can do, it's already going."
"Just override it." "No can do without a manager's code."
"Swap shifts with me?" "No can do this week. Next week, sure."

entries.meaning: A flat statement that the odds are zero. Not a chance is the more common conversational form; adding in hell makes it emphatic and mildly profane.
examples: "Do we still have time to make the 6:40?" "No chance."
"Would you ever go skydiving?" "Not a chance."
"Not a chance in hell he finishes that by Monday."
"Can you talk them down on the price?" "No chance — they've got three other offers."
"Think she'll say yes?" "Not a chance, but ask her anyway."

entries.meaning: From gambling: the roll doesn't count. It refuses a request outright, or reports that an attempt failed, and it carries a friendly, wisecracking, slightly old-fashioned tone.
examples: "Did they give you the refund?" "No dice."
"Can I get an extension on this?" "No dice."
"I tried both passwords — no dice."
"No dice on the reservation. They're booked through October."
"Ask him one more time." "I did. No dice."

entries.meaning: An emphatic, folksy no with an old-fashioned American twang. Nobody says it neutrally anymore; it turns up for comic emphasis or from speakers putting on a deliberate down-home voice. Bob is not anybody in particular.
examples: "Are you ever going back there?" "No siree."
"No siree Bob, I have learned my lesson."
"Did you touch a drop?" "No sir, not one."
"Are we lost?" "No siree — I know exactly where we are."
"You planning to retire?" "No siree. They'll have to carry me out."

entries.meaning: The workhorse emphatic refusal. It also does double duty as an expression of disbelief — No way! said fast and rising means "I can't believe it" — so tone and context decide which one a listener hears. No way José (/hoʊˈzeɪ/, hoh-ZAY) is a rhyming intensifier and sounds playful, even childish.
examples: "Can you cover my shift Saturday?" "No way, I've got a wedding."
"No way am I paying that much for a haircut."
"Let me guess — you told him yes?" "No way."
"Can I have a bite?" "No way José."
"They want the whole thing redone by tomorrow." "No way in hell that happens."

entries.meaning: An absolute refusal, staked on the other person's life for emphasis. It is a little theatrical and a little dated, which makes it handy when you want the refusal to be final but good-humored.
examples: "Are you going to let him borrow the boat?" "Not on your life."
"Would you eat that?" "Not on your life."
"Not on your life — I've seen how he drives."
"Any chance you'd move back to Ohio?" "Not on your life."
"You'd tell me if you knew, wouldn't you?" "Not on your life."

entries.meaning: An old-fashioned refusal meaning "that is not going to happen." It has a 1940s newsroom flavor and now reads as deliberately vintage, though plenty of older Americans still use it perfectly straight.
examples: "Can we stay up till midnight?" "Nothing doing."
"I asked about a discount — nothing doing."
"Nothing doing, kid. Back of the line."
"Will they take a check?" "Nothing doing. Cash only."
"I tried to talk him out of it, but nothing doing."

entries.meaning: A refusal that declares the proposal not even eligible for discussion. It is the formal register's strongest no, and it comes naturally from parents, officials, and anybody with the authority to close a topic.
examples: "Could we push the launch to June?" "Out of the question."
"A refund at this point is out of the question."
"Can I go alone?" "Absolutely out of the question."
"That's out of the question," the judge said. "Next matter."
"What about hiring two more people?" "Out of the question — the budget's frozen."

entries.meaning: The most theatrical refusal in ordinary use: the thing can only happen once the speaker is dead. It is almost always hyperbole, and it usually defends something the speaker feels protective of.
examples: "They want to tear down the old library." "Over my dead body."
"He's planning to name the baby Ragnar." "Over my dead body."
"Over my dead body are they putting a parking lot there."
"Can I get a tattoo?" "Over my dead body."
"They think they can take the case away from me." "Over my dead body."

entries.meaning: Says the day in question is never coming. It answers a prediction or a promise by pretending to look forward to it, and the fake eagerness is the whole joke — which is why it is usually delivered with a little laugh in front of it.
examples: "He says he's going to start doing his own laundry." "That'll be the day."
"Maybe the trains will run on time this winter." "That'll be the day."
"That'll be the day — she hasn't apologized to anybody since I've known her."
"One of these years they'll fix the roof." "Ha. That'll be the day."
"You might even end up liking it." "That'll be the day."

entries.meaning: Answers "when?" with an impossible date, meaning never. It is the standard American way to refuse or to dismiss a prediction while turning the whole thing into a joke.
examples: "When is he going to clean out the garage?" "When pigs fly."
"They'll fix it eventually." "Yeah, when pigs fly."
"When hell freezes over — that's when I'll set foot in that place again."
"Are you ever going to learn to swim?" "When pigs fly."
"She said she'd think about it." "Sure, and she'll get back to you when pigs fly."

entries.meaning: A taunting refusal aimed at the wanting rather than at the request: not merely no, but you'd love that, wouldn't you. It needs enough closeness to tease — said to a stranger or across a power gap it stops being funny immediately.
examples: "I figured you'd give me the window seat." "You wish."
"Admit it, you missed me." "You wish."
"So I'm off dish duty tonight?" "You wish."
"You wish," he said, and slid the last slice out of reach.
"She's going to say yes, I can feel it." "You wish."

entries.meaning: Rejects a suggestion as laughably unlikely — it is short for "as if that would ever happen." The phrase carries a strong 1990s Valley-girl flavor from the movie Clueless, and Americans who use it now are usually winking at that history.
examples: "He probably thinks you're going to apologize." "As if."
"You could just ask her out." "As if."
"As if I'd let you drive after that."
"They said the wait is only ten minutes." "As if."
"I heard you two are getting back together." "As if!"

entries.meaning: Sarcastic acceptance of an explanation the speaker does not believe for a second. The word likely is doing exactly the opposite of its literal work, and the phrase almost always comes with a raised eyebrow.
examples: "The dog ate it." "Likely story."
"Traffic was terrible." "A likely story."
"Likely story — you told me the same thing last month."
"I was just passing by and thought I'd stop in." "Likely story."
"He says the transfer never went through." "Likely story."

entries.meaning: Mock praise for an attempt that did not work — a lie you saw through, an excuse you are not accepting, an offer that was never going to fly. The sincere version, said to somebody who genuinely tried, rises at the end and comes with warmth; the dismissive one is flat and leaves a small pause after it. Good one does the same job for a claim so unlikely that the speaker treats it as a joke.
examples: "I sent it days ago — must have gone to your spam." "Nice try."
"Nice try. Bedtime is still eight o'clock."
"I thought the deadline was next week." "Nice try, it's been on the calendar since June."
"Would you take four hundred for it?" "Nice try."
"The dog unplugged the router." "Good one."

entries.meaning: Scoffing dismissal of a claim, an excuse, or a bit of theater: "you cannot expect me to take that seriously." Note that polite please and dismissive please are the same word — the sarcastic one is lower, longer, and usually has oh in front of it. The joke spelling puh-leeze (/pəˈliz/) exists to make that drawl visible in writing.
examples: "He said he was too busy to call." "Oh please."
"I'm probably going to fail this class." "Please. You have an A."
"Oh please, you love the attention."
"This is the worst day of my life." "Puh-leeze. You spilled a coffee."
"She's basically a professional." "Oh please, she took two lessons."

entries.meaning: Sarcastic okay pretends to accept what was just said while signaling that the speaker believes none of it and intends to do nothing about it. In writing the flatness has to be spelled out: a period after Okay. or a bare k in a text both read as cold and dismissive, which is why they start arguments.
examples: "I'll have it to you by Friday, I promise." "Okay."
"Okayyy, sure, whatever you say."
"I'm the most organized person in this house." "Okay."
She texted back a single k and he knew he was in trouble.
"You're going to run a marathon in June." "Okay. Let's see."

entries.meaning: Drawn out and falling in pitch, right means the speaker does not believe you at all. The stretched spelling riiight exists precisely because ordinary right — which means sincere agreement — would be read the wrong way on the page.
examples: "He's quitting to become a professional poker player." "Riiight."
"I never touched it." "Right."
"Riiight, and I'm the Queen of England."
"She says the check is in the mail." "Right. Sure it is."
"This will only take five minutes." "Riiight."

entries.meaning: A challenge to the authority behind a claim: "who exactly decided that?" It is combative — halfway between a question and a shove — and it dares the other person to produce a source or back down.
examples: "You can't park here." "Says who?"
"Nobody wears those anymore." "Says who?"
"Says who? Show me where it says that in the lease."
"You're too old for that." "Says who?"
"The deal's off." "Sez who?"

entries.meaning: Said flat or drawn out, sure is disbelief wearing the costume of agreement. The sincere sure is quick and rises slightly; the sarcastic one is slow, level or falling, and often followed by a pointed little pause.
examples: "I was going to call you." "Suuure you were."
"It's completely safe." "Sure it is."
"He says he read the whole contract." "Sure."
"I'll be there at six sharp." "Sure, sure."
"This is the last time, I swear." "Sure, that's what you said in March."

entries.meaning: An internet-born way of humoring somebody whose claim is obviously untrue, from a line in a Brady Bunch movie. It is playful and at home in group chats and comment threads; it can sting badly if aimed at somebody being sincere, and it simply confuses anyone who does not know the reference.
examples: "I only had one slice." "Sure, Jan."
"He says the traffic app was wrong." "Sure, Jan."
"I'm going to start waking up at five every day." "Sure, Jan."
Somebody in the comments replied with a flat sure, Jan and the thread died right there.
"I could've gone pro if I hadn't hurt my knee." "Sure, Jan."

entries.respell: uh-HUH (the sarcastic version is flat and level, UH-huh)
entries.meaning: Uh-huh normally means yes, or "I'm still listening." Said flat and slow with no rise at the end, it means the exact opposite: "I hear you, and I don't buy a word of it." Nothing but intonation separates the two, which makes it one of the easiest interjections in English to be misread on.
examples: "I'll get to it first thing tomorrow." "Uh-huh."
"It was already broken when I found it." "Uh-huh."
"Uh-huh. And where exactly were you until two in the morning?"
"I read the entire thing." "Uh-huh, sure you did."
"We're just friends." "Mm-hmm."

entries.meaning: The standard American sarcastic dismissal: two words of agreement that together mean "I don't believe that for a second." The stress lands hard on right and the pitch falls; said with a rise the same words would be genuine agreement, which is why the run-together yeah right is the usual spelling for the sarcastic one.
examples: "He says he's going to be here on time." "Yeah right."
"The repair should be covered under warranty." "Yeah right."
"Yeah right, like they're going to refund the whole thing."
"I'm quitting sugar for a year." "Yeah, right."
"She told me she's never once been late." "Yeah right, I've worked with her."

entries.register: dated (1920s slang; now purely a period costume)
entries.meaning: Jazz-age slang for nonsense, and especially for flattery — from the boardinghouse trick of filling out a cheap meal with a dish of applesauce. It is dead in ordinary speech and survives only where somebody is deliberately doing a 1920s voice.
examples: "Applesauce. He has never set foot in a courtroom."
"He told her she was the most beautiful girl in Chicago." "Applesauce."
"Applesauce! You'll believe anything a man in a good hat tells you."
"The ad says you'll double your money inside a year." "Applesauce."
"Applesauce," she said, and snapped her compact shut.

entries.meaning: "That is complete nonsense," delivered in a deliberately old-fashioned voice. Almost no American under sixty says it straight; it survives as a comic, blustery exclamation and as the name of a party word game.
examples: "Balderdash! I have never heard such a ridiculous theory."
"They claim the recipe is three hundred years old." "Balderdash."
"Balderdash, sir. You have no evidence whatsoever."
"He says the property line runs right through the oak tree." "Balderdash."
"Balderdash!" my grandfather said, and switched off the television.

entries.meaning: The friendly American word for nonsense, spelled off the sausage. It calls a claim false without any vulgarity, which is why it shows up in politics and on the evening news in places where bull would never make it to air.
examples: "Baloney. That is not what the contract says."
"They say prices went up because of shipping costs." "Baloney."
"Baloney! You've been telling that story for years and it gets better every time."
"He claims he never got the message." "That's baloney — I watched him read it."
"You're too old to start over." "Baloney."

entries.meaning: A clipped Victorian exclamation meaning nonsense, borrowed from Turkish boş, "empty." It is essentially extinct in American speech and lives on in old novels and period dialogue.
examples: "Bosh! The man is a fraud and everybody knows it."
"She says the house is haunted." "Bosh."
"Bosh and nonsense. Sit down and eat your dinner."
"They warned us the bridge was unsafe." "Bosh — it's stood a hundred years."
"Bosh!" he snorted, folding up the newspaper.

entries.meaning: The clipped, sayable-in-company form of bullshit: it flatly calls a statement a lie. B.S. is the initialed version and is milder still, while bull hockey and bullcrap are jokey minced forms that keep the shape and lose the profanity.
examples: "Bull. You have never run a five-minute mile in your life."
"They said the fee is non-negotiable." "That's bull."
"B.S., and you know it."
"He told everyone the whole thing was his idea." "What a bunch of bull."
"Bull hockey," my uncle said. "That fish was ten pounds, tops."

entries.meaning: The strongest common way to call something a lie or a sham. This is genuine profanity — fine among friends, a real problem in a workplace, a classroom, or anything on the record. It has a second use worth knowing: it protests unfairness ("that's not right") as well as falsehood.
examples: "Bullshit. I was standing right there."
"They're charging a fifty-dollar cancellation fee." "That's bullshit."
"Bullshit — nobody told us the deadline moved."
"He says the numbers were audited." "Bullshit they were."
"You had to have known about this." "Bullshit, I found out this morning like everyone else."

entries.meaning: Nonsense, especially empty talk dressed up as fact. It shortens buncombe, named for a North Carolina congressman's famously windy speech, and it is the root of debunk — the form most Americans now meet first.
examples: "Bunk. There's no study that says any such thing."
"The whole detox thing is bunk."
"They claim it cures a cold in a day." "Bunk."
"Pure bunkum," the professor said, "and expensive bunkum at that."
"He gave us the usual speech about family values." "Bunk, all of it."

entries.register: very informal (from African American English; spoken and internet/text)
entries.meaning: The one young, living member of the nonsense family. Cap is a lie, and calling cap on a claim says you do not believe it. It comes from African American English, where capping is boasting or exaggerating. Among friends it is a challenge rather than a real accusation — but it belongs to speakers under about thirty, and in an older mouth it sounds borrowed.
examples: "I ran a five-minute mile in high school." "Cap."
"That's cap and you know it."
"He says he's never been late to anything in his life." "Cap."
"Stop capping — you did not talk to the manager."
"I paid forty bucks for these." "Cap. They're two hundred online."

entries.meaning: Showy, empty talk designed to draw a reaction — the word began as theater slang for a line written to trap applause. It is aimed at speeches, ad copy, and editorials rather than at one false statement, and it accuses the speaker of pandering as much as of lying.
examples: "Claptrap. Not one of those numbers is real."
"The closing argument was pure claptrap."
"Utter claptrap, and the room ate it up."
"He finished with something about how we're all family here." "Claptrap."
"Claptrap," she wrote in the margin, and underlined it twice.

entries.meaning: The middle rung between bull and bullshit: it calls a claim a lie or a piece of junk with real coarseness, but stops short of full profanity. Most Americans will say it in front of friends and coworkers and not in front of a client, a classroom, or their grandmother. It has a separate life as a standalone curse at bad news, which is a different job entirely.
examples: "Crap. That is not what the policy says."
"They're calling it a manufacturing defect." "That's crap — the thing's been recalled twice."
"He fed them a load of crap about a family emergency."
"So you pay the fee twice?" "Yep. It's crap."
"The report blames the weather for the delay." "Crap. It sat on somebody's desk for three weeks."

entries.register: informal (the full form a crock of shit is vulgar)
entries.meaning: Almost always used with a: a crock is a claim with nothing in it. It is the front half of a crock of shit, and everybody who hears the short version knows the long one, which gives it more bite than baloney and less than bull.
examples: "What a crock. They knew about the leak in March."
"They're calling it a voluntary contribution." "That's a crock."
"A crock, start to finish — read the fine print."
"He says the decision came down from corporate." "What a crock. He made the call himself."
"Everybody gets an equal shot at the promotion." "Oh, that's a crock."

entries.meaning: A gentle, old-fashioned exclamation that does two jobs: it dismisses a claim as nonsense, and it works as a very mild substitute for a curse when something goes wrong. It sounds like somebody's grandmother, which is exactly why younger speakers reach for it as a joke.
examples: "Fiddlesticks! You are not one bit too old to dance."
"The doctor said I should rest for a week." "Fiddlesticks."
"Fiddlesticks, I dropped the whole tray."
"It's supposed to rain all weekend." "Fiddlesticks."
"She insists she can't cook." "Fiddle-faddle — she made this pie."

entries.meaning: Nineteenth-century American nonsense, and one of the silliest-sounding words in the whole family — which is the only reason it is still around. Nobody picks it to be taken seriously; it is picked for the noise it makes.
examples: "Flapdoodle. The man has never balanced a checkbook in his life."
"He gave a whole speech about destiny." "Flapdoodle."
"Pure flapdoodle, dressed up with a chart."
"The label says it 'supports healthy energy.'" "Flapdoodle."
"Flapdoodle!" she said, and went right on rolling out the dough.

entries.meaning: Nonsense, named for the slop fed to pigs. It is stronger and more contemptuous than baloney but still perfectly clean, which makes it a favorite in op-eds, congressional hearings, and letters to the editor.
examples: "Hogwash. The report says the exact opposite."
"They're calling it a safety measure." "Hogwash — it's about money."
"Pure hogwash, and everybody in that room knew it."
"He says the delay was completely out of their control." "Hogwash."
"Hogwash!" she said. "I've been doing this for thirty years."

entries.meaning: Nonsense of the crowd-pleasing kind — showy, sentimental claims that sound wonderful and mean nothing. It started as show-business slang for cheap emotional tricks and still carries a whiff of the carnival tent.
examples: "Hokum. Nobody loses thirty pounds in a week."
"The whole speech was hokum."
"They dressed it up with charts, but it's hokum."
"He says the machine realigns your energy field." "Hokum, start to finish."
"Hokum," the old critic wrote, "beautifully performed."

entries.meaning: Nonsense — an American coinage from the 1920s that still sounds cheerfully old-timey. It is mild enough for any company, and it usually arrives with a bunch of in front of it.
examples: "Hooey. You can't catch a cold from being cold."
"That's a bunch of hooey and you know it."
"They say the new formula works twice as fast." "Hooey."
"Pure hooey, if you ask me."
"He's been feeding you hooey since the day you met him."

entries.meaning: A 1920s minced substitute for a barnyard vulgarity, meaning nonsense. It survives as a period joke — a Marx Brothers movie title, the sort of thing a cartoon grandfather says — and horse hockey pulls the same trick with the same intent.
examples: "Horsefeathers! That's the oldest excuse in the book."
"He says he built the whole deck himself." "Horsefeathers."
"Horse hockey. I was in the room when they voted."
"They told us the recipe is a family secret." "Horsefeathers — it's on the back of the box."
"Horsefeathers," Grandpa said, waving his hand at the screen.

entries.meaning: A fraud or a piece of empty pretense, and as an exclamation a scornful "nonsense." For Americans it is now almost inseparable from Scrooge's Bah, humbug!, so it reads as Christmas-grumpy more than anything else.
examples: "Bah, humbug. I'm not putting up lights this year."
"Humbug! The man is a salesman, not a healer."
"They call it a tradition. I call it humbug."
"The whole ceremony struck him as humbug."
"Aren't you even a little excited?" "Humbug."

entries.meaning: Insincere talk, exaggeration, nonsense. It is warm and folksy rather than harsh, and it has had a long second life in American politics as a clean way to call an opponent a liar on live television.
examples: "Malarkey. That is not how the tax works."
"A bunch of malarkey, if you ask me."
"He promised everybody a raise by summer." "Malarkey."
"Pure malarkey — I looked it up while he was still talking."
"Don't give me that malarkey about the traffic."

entries.meaning: A tag hung on the end of somebody else's words to throw them back as nonsense: repeat the claim, add my eye, and the claim is dead. It works exactly like my foot and is a shade more old-fashioned.
examples: "Antique, my eye. They're making these in Ohio."
"Free upgrade my eye — they charged us for the bags."
"My eye he did. He wasn't even in town that week."
"Doctor's orders, my eye. He just wants the afternoon off."
"Best in the city, my eye."

entries.meaning: Tacked onto the end of a phrase you are quoting back, my foot rejects it as nonsense. It is the clean member of the family — my eye is older, my ass is vulgar — and it is a staple in the mouths of parents and grandparents.
examples: "Too sick for school, my foot. You were fine ten minutes ago."
"Sold out, my foot. I can see three empty tables from here."
"My foot it's the last one. There's a whole case in the back."
"Vintage, my foot. That's from last season."
"He said it was an honest mistake." "Honest mistake, my foot."

entries.meaning: The plain, all-purpose word for "that is not true," usable in any register from a boardroom to a kitchen table. It has a second, warmer use: brushing aside somebody's self-criticism or their polite refusal of a favor, where it means "don't be silly."
examples: "Nonsense. The numbers have been public for a month."
"I'm probably imposing." "Nonsense, stay for dinner."
"Utter nonsense, and the study says so on page one."
"He claims the policy has always been in place." "Nonsense."
"I'd only slow you down." "Nonsense — come with us."

entries.meaning: Two jobs: a scornful "nonsense," and a mild expression of disgust or disappointment. It comes from Yiddish and German pfui, and it is cartoonish and gentle enough to say in front of children.
examples: "Phooey. I don't believe a word of it."
"The game got rained out." "Phooey."
"Phooey on the diet — pass the cake."
"They say you have to book a year in advance." "Phooey."
"Phooey!" she said when the machine ate her dollar.

entries.meaning: Trivial nonsense — not a dangerous lie, just empty, silly talk. It is prim and bookish, and an American who reaches for it is almost always being funny on purpose.
examples: "Piffle. Nobody was ever harmed by a little rain."
"He wrote three pages about the font." "Piffle."
"What piffle," she said, dropping the magazine on the table.
"They say the color of the walls affects your mood." "Piffle."
"Piffle and nonsense. Get in the car."

entries.meaning: A blustery "nonsense," from a Dutch dialect phrase considerably less polite than it sounds in English. Americans keep it alive mostly for its comic sound, and it pairs naturally with an indignant older speaker.
examples: "Poppycock! I have never heard anything so absurd."
"They say the recipe can't be duplicated." "Poppycock."
"Pure poppycock, every bit of it."
"He claims that tree is two hundred years old." "Poppycock — I planted it."
"Poppycock," the senator said, and the hearing room laughed.

entries.meaning: "Nonsense" — the British-flavored member of the family. Americans understand it perfectly and do use it, but it always sounds slightly imported, so choosing it is a style decision rather than the default.
examples: "Rubbish. The train was on time all week."
"Utter rubbish, and he knows it."
"They say the recipe is the authentic one." "Rubbish."
"He told the reporters he had no idea." "Rubbish."
"What rubbish — I read the same article and it says the opposite."

entries.meaning: Utter nonsense, from British schoolboy slang in which tommy meant foolish. It is thoroughly archaic in American speech and now shows up mainly in historical fiction or as a deliberate flourish.
examples: "Tommyrot! No such rule has ever existed."
"He says a gentleman never carries cash." "Tommyrot."
"Tommyrot, from beginning to end."
"They warned that the machines would replace us all." "Tommyrot."
"Tommyrot," the headmaster snapped. "Back to your rooms."

entries.meaning: Silly, empty talk — nonsense that is more tiresome than dishonest. It is bookish, and it is usually aimed at a piece of writing or a speech rather than at a single false statement.
examples: "Twaddle. The man has never read a page of it."
"The whole editorial was sentimental twaddle."
"Utter twaddle, dressed up in long words."
"They call it a philosophy of leadership." "Twaddle."
"Twaddle," she muttered, skipping ahead to the last chapter.

entries.meaning: A grumpy grunt of dismissal — contempt for an idea, an offer, or the general state of the world. It sounds theatrical and old to American ears, and it is now heard mostly in its Scrooge collocation.
examples: "Bah. I've got no use for any of it."
"The concert's sold out." "Bah."
"Bah, humbug," he said, and went back to his crossword.
"Aren't you going to congratulate him?" "Bah."
"Bah! Let the young ones worry about it."

entries.meaning: Tells somebody to drop a pretense: stop exaggerating, stop pretending, stop the act. It accuses more directly than come on — the other person is not merely wrong, they are putting it on.
examples: "Come off it. You've known about this for weeks."
"I had no idea it would cost that much." "Oh, come off it."
"Come off it, you're not seriously offended."
"He says he's never had a drink in his life." "Come off it."
"I'm the only one who does anything around here." "Come off it, Dave."

entries.meaning: Protests something as unreasonable or unbelievable: "you cannot be serious." Come on also lives elsewhere as encouragement (come on, you've got this) and as impatience (come on, we're late), so the skeptical sense depends entirely on a falling, exasperated delivery.
examples: "The fee is one hundred dollars." "Oh, come on."
"Come on, nobody actually believes that."
"He says he did it all himself." "C'mon. He had six people helping."
"You have to admit she had a point." "Come on, she was making it up as she went."
"They're calling that a foul?" "Come on!"

entries.meaning: A one-word verdict that something probably will not happen or probably is not true. It is cooler and more measured than the sarcastic options, which makes it one of the few items here that works in writing and at work.
examples: "Will the shipment make it before the holiday?" "Doubtful."
"Do you think they'll appeal?" "Highly doubtful."
"Doubtful — the forecast has it raining all weekend."
"Any chance he still remembers me?" "Doubtful, it's been fifteen years."
"Is that going to come in under budget?" "Very doubtful."

entries.meaning: Corrects a wrong impression by putting the truth at the other end of the scale: not merely "no," but "no, and the reverse." It usually follows a bare negative and it stays calm, which makes it one of the few items in this category that is safe in writing and at work.
examples: "So you're unhappy with the numbers?" "Far from it — they beat the projection."
"Was he rude about it?" "No. Far from it."
"I assume that settles the matter." "Far from it."
"It sounds like the trip was a disaster." "Far from it, actually. We had a great time."
"Is the job getting any easier?" "Far from it."

entries.meaning: Exasperated rejection of a claim, an excuse, or an unreasonable demand. Depending on the tone it also means "stop criticizing me" — the same words, aimed at the other person's pressure rather than at their honesty.
examples: "He says he was too busy to send one text." "Give me a break."
"Gimme a break — that's a two-hundred-dollar cable."
"You should have caught that typo." "Give me a break, I was proofreading at midnight."
"They're calling it a luxury studio." "Oh, give me a break. It's a closet."
"She claims she's never seen the show." "Give me a break, she quotes it constantly."

entries.register: formal — but so old-fashioned that most Americans now use it jokingly
entries.meaning: A stiffly courteous way to contradict somebody. The politeness is genuine and so is the disagreement, but the formality has aged to the point where the phrase mostly arrives with a raised eyebrow — the stuffiness is the joke. In a setting that really is formal, I respectfully disagree is what people actually say.
examples: "Nobody reads the manual." "I beg to differ. I read it twice."
"That's the best pizza in the state." "I beg to differ."
"I beg to differ, counselor. The statute says otherwise."
"Everyone came out of that meeting happy." "I'd beg to differ."
"You have never once done the dishes." "I beg to differ," he said, holding up a sponge.

entries.meaning: A plain, polite way to say you do not believe something will happen or is true. It is the safest skeptical response in this entire category: no sarcasm, no slang, nothing that could be heard as rude.
examples: "Do you think they'll even notice?" "I doubt it."
"He'll probably call tonight." "I doubt it."
"I seriously doubt it — that model was discontinued years ago."
"Is there any parking left?" "I doubt it, but let's drive by."
"They say the price will come down after the holidays." "I highly doubt it."

entries.meaning: Contradicts a statement with force: "that is absolutely not so." It usually echoes the claim it is denying (like hell he did), and it can also throw an order straight back (like hell I will). Mild profanity — keep it out of the office.
examples: "He paid for everything." "Like hell he did."
"You're going to apologize to her." "Like hell I am."
"Like hell it was an accident."
"They said the store closes at nine." "Like hell — the sign says eight."
"You're staying home tonight." "Like hell."

entries.meaning: The vulgar member of the my foot / my eye family: repeat the claim, add my ass, and you have called it a lie in the strongest everyday terms available. Genuinely profane — friends and bars, not offices and classrooms.
examples: "Best deal in town, my ass."
"Emergency meeting, my ass. He wanted an audience."
"My ass it's under warranty."
"He says he's retiring." "Retiring, my ass."
"It's a nonprofit, my ass — look at those salaries."

entries.meaning: Rejects a statement and installs its opposite in one move. It belongs to written and prepared English — a brief, a letter, a debate, a witness who has thought about the answer — and in casual conversation it comes off as either stuffy or deliberately arch.
examples: "You seem to think the policy failed." "On the contrary. It did exactly what it was built to do."
"On the contrary, the numbers have been consistent for six quarters."
"I take it you object." "Quite the contrary — I'm in favor."
"The witness was uncooperative, then." "On the contrary, Your Honor."
"So the rain ruined the whole weekend." "On the contrary, it was the best part."

entries.ipa: no standard IPA — a short puff of air through nearly closed lips, roughly /pf(t)/, with no vowel
entries.meaning: The written form of a dismissive little raspberry: an exhale meaning "that is not worth taking seriously." It waves off a claim, a threat, or a worry with almost no effort at all, and the effortlessness is part of the insult.
examples: "Pfft. That's not even a real rule."
"He said he could beat you at chess." "Pfft."
"Pfft, I've fixed worse than this with duct tape."
"Aren't you nervous about the presentation?" "Pfft. No."
"They think a two-hour drive is far." "Pfft."

entries.respell: psh — a soft sh with a puff in front and no vowel; the spelled-out older form pshaw is /ʃɔ/, SHAW
entries.meaning: A scoffing hiss of dismissal, close to pfft but a shade more contemptuous and more often aimed at a person than at an idea. Pshaw is the nineteenth-century spelling and now sounds theatrical or rural.
examples: "Psh. He's not going to say anything."
"You'll need a reservation." "Psh, on a Tuesday?"
"Pssh, that's nothing. Wait till you see mine."
"She thinks she's the best player here." "Psh."
"Pshaw," said the old man. "In my day we walked."

entries.meaning: Challenges a claim that something is a rule, a habit, or a settled fact: the speaker never agreed to it and would like to know where it came from. It is close kin to says who, and it lands as a shove even when the tone is light — which is why it is a bad answer to give a police officer or a boss.
examples: "We don't allow outside food." "Since when?"
"You hate cilantro." "Since when? I put it on everything."
"Since when do we need approval for a fifty-dollar order?"
"He's in charge of the schedule now." "Since when?"
"It's a black-tie thing." "Since when? I wore jeans last year."
